claim: Epilepsy has an estimated prevalence of 50 million worldwide.
source: Epilepsy is one of the most common neurological disorders with an estimated prevalence of 50 million worldwide (World Health Organization, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization, 2020.

claim: Seizures are defined as a transient occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain.
source: It is characterized by spontaneously recurring seizures, which are 'a transient occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain' (Fisher et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fisher et al., 2005.

claim: Current knowledge is insufficient to form a scientifically based classification of seizures according to the International League Against Epilepsy.
source: In its latest position paper, the International League Against Epilepsy states: 'Because current knowledge is insufficient to form a scientifically based classification, the 2017 Classification is operational (practical)' (Fisher et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fisher et al., 2017.

claim: Seizures are characterized by abrupt changes in the EEG waveform at seizure onset and offset.
source: The basis of TSD is the observation that seizures are characterized by abrupt changes in the EEG waveform at seizure onset and offset, which we interpreted as bifurcations known from dynamic system theory (Lopes da Silva et al., 2003a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lopes da Silva et al., 2003a.

claim: There are only six types of bifurcations involved in bursting in systems with two variables.
source: Two variables are the minimum necessary to generate oscillations, and in systems with two variables, there are only six types of bifurcations involved in bursting (Figure 1, for further details also see Saggio et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to Figure 1 and a citation to Saggio et al., 2017.

claim: Four bifurcations can be used to enter the bursting regime, and another four to exit, giving a total of 16 possible dynamotypes.
source: Four can be used to enter the bursting regime, and another four to exit, giving a total of 16 possible dynamotypes (Izhikevich, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Izhikevich, 2000.

claim: One seizure offset bifurcation was present across multiple species, brain regions, and pathologies, including a small cohort of humans.
source: Generalizing this to epilepsy, (Jirsa et al., 2014) proposed the existence of 16 theoretically possible dynamotypes (i.e. seizure types), and found one seizure offset bifurcation that was present across multiple species, brain regions, and pathologies, including a small cohort of humans.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jirsa et al., 2014.

claim: Over 2000 focal-onset seizures from multiple centers were analyzed to identify bifurcations at onset and offset.
source: Analyzing over 2000 focal-onset seizures from multiple centers, we find evidence of all 16 dynamotypes predicted in TSD.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the analysis performed in the manuscript.

claim: All 16 dynamotypes predicted in TSD were found in the analyzed seizures.
source: Analyzing over 2000 focal-onset seizures from multiple centers, we find evidence of all 16 dynamotypes predicted in TSD.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the analysis performed in the manuscript.

claim: Patients' dynamotypes evolve during their lifetime.
source: We demonstrate that patients' dynamotypes evolve during their lifetime and display complex but systematic variations including hierarchy (certain types are more common), non-bijectivity (a patient may display multiple types) and pairing preference (multiple types may occur during one seizure).
evidence: The claim is supported by the demonstration in the manuscript.

claim: Patients display complex but systematic variations in dynamotypes including hierarchy, non-bijectivity, and pairing preference.
source: We demonstrate that patients' dynamotypes evolve during their lifetime and display complex but systematic variations including hierarchy (certain types are more common), non-bijectivity (a patient may display multiple types) and pairing preference (multiple types may occur during one seizure).
evidence: The claim is supported by the demonstration in the manuscript.

claim: Seizures were analyzed from 120 patients recorded on intracranial EEG in seven centers worldwide.
source: We analyzed seizures from 120 patients recorded on intracranial EEG in seven centers worldwide (Appendix I.1) (Ihle et al., 2012; Cook et al., 2013; Kanazawa et al., 2015; Wagenaar et al., 2015) to identify the bifurcations at onset and offset.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the patient cohort and citations to the data sources.

claim: All patients analyzed had focal onset seizures.
source: All patients had focal onset seizures.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the manuscript.

claim: In the supercritical Hopf bifurcation, the amplitude of the oscillations starts at zero and increases proportionally to the square root of the distance from the bifurcation point.
source: in the supercritical Hopf bifurcation (SupH), the amplitude of the oscillations starts at zero and increases proportionally to the square root of the distance from the bifurcation point
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in bifurcation theory and is cited in the manuscript (Strogatz, 2015).

claim: The Saddle-Node on an Invariant Circle (SNIC) bifurcation has oscillations that increase in frequency as the square-root of the distance from the bifurcation point.
source: the Saddle-Node on an Invariant Circle (SNIC) bifurcation has oscillations that increase in frequency as the square-root of the same distance.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in bifurcation theory and is cited in the manuscript (Strogatz, 2015).

claim: Saddle-Node (SN) and subcritical Hopf (SubH) bifurcations have abrupt amplitude and frequency changes that do not follow specific scaling laws.
source: The other two, Saddle-Node (SN) and subcritical Hopf (SubH) bifurcations, have abrupt amplitude and frequency changes that do not follow specific scaling laws.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in bifurcation theory.

claim: The SN bifurcation can contain a jump in the signal baseline (DC shift).
source: The SN can contain a jump in the signal baseline (i.e. direct current (DC) shift), but in the absence of a detectable DC shift these two types can be difficult to distinguish even theoretically.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in bifurcation theory.

claim: SN without DC shift and SubH are difficult to distinguish even theoretically.
source: but in the absence of a detectable DC shift these two types can be difficult to distinguish even theoretically.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical considerations in bifurcation theory.

claim: The SNIC bifurcation at offset is characterized by decreasing frequency following square-root scaling.
source: Two of the bifurcations are characterized by decreasing frequency, following square-root scaling for the SNIC and logarithmic scaling for the Saddle-Homoclinic (SH) bifurcation.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in bifurcation theory.

claim: The Saddle-Homoclinic (SH) bifurcation at offset is characterized by decreasing frequency following logarithmic scaling.
source: Two of the bifurcations are characterized by decreasing frequency, following square-root scaling for the SNIC and logarithmic scaling for the Saddle-Homoclinic (SH) bifurcation.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in bifurcation theory.

claim: Slowing at seizure termination is a well-known clinical hallmark of a seizure.
source: Both these dynamics manifest as slowing of the seizure down to zero near its end, which is the well-known clinical hallmark of a seizure (St. Louis and Frey, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to St. Louis and Frey, 2016.

claim: Slowing at seizure termination has been identified as an inherent characteristic of seizures across all spatial scales.
source: This 'slowing' at seizure termination has been identified as an inherent characteristic of seizures across all spatial scales (Kramer et al., 2012), and in multiple species and brain regions (Jirsa et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kramer et al., 2012 and Jirsa et al., 2014.

claim: It is difficult to distinguish between SNIC and SH scaling laws when using only frequency of spikes due to the small number of spikes near the end of seizures.
source: Due to the small number of spikes near the end of seizures, it is difficult to distinguish between these two scaling laws when using only frequency of spikes (Jirsa et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jirsa et al., 2014.

claim: The SupH bifurcation at offset has square-root-scaled decreasing amplitude and no scaling law for the frequency.
source: The other two bifurcations do not require slowing at termination: the SupH bifurcation with square-root-scaled decreasing amplitude and no scaling law for the frequency
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in bifurcation theory.

claim: The Fold Limit Cycle (FLC) bifurcation has no specific scaling law for either frequency or amplitude.
source: and the Fold Limit Cycle (FLC) that has no specific scaling law for either frequency or amplitude.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in bifurcation theory.

claim: Only the SH bifurcation can have a DC shift at offset.
source: Note that these two offset types may appear somewhat atypical to a clinician, as 'slowing down' is expected at the end of most seizures. The only dependence on a DC shift is that only the SH can have a shift
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in bifurcation theory.

claim: Human reviewers were more reliable than the automated algorithm in noisy clinical data.
source: In addition, we found that human reviewers were more reliable than the automated algorithm in noisy clinical data.
evidence: The claim is supported by the comparison performed in the manuscript.

claim: 41% of seizures in patients with DC recordings started with constant amplitude spikes and a DC shift, signifying SN bifurcation.
source: Many seizures (41%) started with constant amplitude spikes and a DC shift, signifying SN bifurcation (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: 37% of seizures in patients with DC recordings had similar amplitude/frequency dynamics without a DC shift (either SubH or SN).
source: The second most frequent was similar amplitude/frequency dynamics without a DC shift (either SubH or SN, 37%)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 14% of seizures in patients with DC recordings had SupH onset.
source: followed by SupH (14%)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 6% of seizures in patients with DC recordings had SNIC onset.
source: and SNIC (6%).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only 1 out of 51 seizures with DC recordings could not be agreed upon by the reviewers for onset classification.
source: and only 1/51 seizures could not be agreed upon by the reviewers.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At least three of the predicted bifurcation types are present at onset in human seizures.
source: Despite the inability to distinguish SN (-DC) and SubH, we demonstrate that at least three of the predicted bifurcation types are present at onset in human seizures.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nearly half of the seizures labeled as SN onset progressed into square-root amplitude scaling after 2–5 s, consistent with a switch to SupH dynamics.
source: For example, nearly half of the seizures labeled as SN onset progressed into square-root amplitude scaling after 2–5 s, consistent with a switch to SupH dynamics
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In non-DC coupled recordings, 67% of seizures were SN-SubH onset.
source: Combining these two into a single group, we found that 67% were SN-SubH
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

source: 26% were SupH
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In non-DC coupled recordings, 6% of seizures were SNIC onset.
source: 6% were SNIC
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 20% of seizures with DC recordings had SH (+DC) offset.
source: Thus, 10/51 (20%) were SH (+DC)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 20% of seizures with DC recordings were potentially SH(-DC) or SNIC offset.
source: while the remaining 10 (20%) were potentially SH(-DC) or SNIC (Figure 2F).

source: The remaining 31 patients did not have slowing at the end of their seizure (53% FLC

source: 6% SupH

source: The majority of seizures had arbitrary ISI and/or amplitude (54% FLC)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 41% of seizures in non-DC coupled data had slowing down characteristic of SH(-DC)-SNIC offset.
source: while 41% had slowing down characteristic of SH(-DC)-SNIC.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 3% of seizures in non-DC coupled data had SupH offset.
source: The remaining seizures either had constant ISI with amplitude that decreased as a square root (SupH, 3%)

claim: 12 different dynamotypes were identified in 49 patients with DC recordings.
source: We identified 12 different dynamotypes, with the limitation that several of the dynamotypes cannot be fully distinguished in the absence of a DC shift (e.g. SH(-DC) – SNIC offsets).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The taxonomy was dominated by seizures with either SN or SubH onsets and slowing (SH-SNIC) or arbitrary dynamics (FLC) at the end.
source: The taxonomy was dominated by seizures with either SN or SubH onsets and slowing (SH-SNIC) or arbitrary dynamics (FLC) at the end.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SupH and SNIC onsets were less common in the cohort of focal onset seizures.
source: In this cohort of focal onset seizures, the SupH and SNIC onsets were less common, accounting for all four dynamotypes that were absent.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There was a correlation between age and seizure dynamotype, with older patients tending to have more SupH onsets.
source: There was a correlation with age, as older patients tended to have more SupH onsets (Appendix I.9).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Appendix I.9.

claim: No correlation was found between seizure dynamotype and patient gender, pathology, or localization.
source: We compared all available clinical metadata from patients with their dynamotype and found no correlation between seizure type and patient gender, pathology, or localization.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No significant similarities were found between the dynamotype and a prior visual classification system.
source: There were no significant similarities between the dynamotype and the visual classification.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: One patient had two consecutive seizures belonging to different types: one supH/supH and one supH/SH.
source: While analyzing this dataset, we noted that one patient had two consecutive seizures belonging to different types: one supH/supH and one supH/SH, raising the possibility that an individual may express different types of seizures.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Over 2000 seizures from 13 patients were analyzed from a unique dataset from Melbourne with continuous intracranial EEG recording for many months.
source: To test whether individuals display different types of seizures over time, we used a unique dataset from Melbourne in which patients had intracranial EEG recorded continuously for many months (Cook et al., 2013). We analyzed over 2000 seizures from 13 patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and a citation to Cook et al., 2013.

claim: All 13 patients expressed at least two offset patterns.
source: As seen in Figure 3, all 13 patients expressed at least two offset patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Individuals have seizures from different dynamotypes over time.
source: Nevertheless, we can unambiguously conclude that individuals have seizures from different dynamotypes over time.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: During seizures, the firing activity of neurons becomes organized, enabling the emergence of oscillatory activity that can be observed in electrographic recordings.
source: During seizures, the firing activity of neurons becomes organized, enabling the emergence of oscillatory activity that can be observed in electrographic recordings.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about seizure dynamics.

claim: The organization of neuronal firing during seizures greatly reduces the degrees of freedom necessary to describe the observed activity.
source: This greatly reduces the degrees of freedom necessary to describe the observed activity, that is a small number of differential equations are sufficient to describe the collective behavior (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in dynamical systems theory and is illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Two variables are the minimum number necessary to produce oscillatory activity.
source: We here consider a system with the minimum number of variables necessary to produce oscillatory activity, two.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in dynamical systems theory.

claim: Two states can be distinguished in the system: resting (fixed point) or oscillatory (limit cycle).
source: Based on the parameter values, two states can be distinguished: resting (fixed point) or oscillatory (limit cycle).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in dynamical systems theory.

claim: When resting and oscillatory states coexist for the same range of parameter values (bistability), transitions between them can be promoted by noise if the system is sufficiently close to a bifurcation.
source: When these two states coexist for the same range of parameter values (bistability), transitions between them can be promoted by noise if the system is sufficiently close to a bifurcation (Lopes da Silva et al., 2003a; Kalitzin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lopes da Silva et al., 2003a and Kalitzin et al., 2010.

claim: The statistics of ictal durations point to the existence of a deterministic process governing the transition for seizure offset and possibly for the onset.
source: However, the statistics of ictal durations (Suffczynski et al., 2006) points to the existence of a deterministic process governing this transition for seizure offset and possibly for the onset.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Suffczynski et al., 2006.

claim: A deterministic transition can be achieved with the addition of a third variable acting on the timescale of ictal duration.
source: This can be achieved with the addition of a third variable acting on the timescale of ictal duration.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical reasoning in dynamical systems.

claim: The 'Epileptor' is a set of five differential equations able to account for the most dominant dynamotype (SN/SH).
source: We previously validated this approach with the 'Epileptor,' a set of five differential equations able to account for the most dominant dynamotype (Jirsa et al., 2014) (SN/SH, also known as 'square-wave' bursting Rinzel, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jirsa et al., 2014 and Rinzel, 1987.

claim: In the Epileptor, the transition from 'normal' to seizure state and back again, as well as the seizure dynamics, are controlled by a collective permittivity variable that evolves on a slow time scale.
source: In the Epileptor, the transition from 'normal' to seizure state and back again, as well as the seizure dynamics, are controlled by a collective permittivity variable that evolves on a slow time scale.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the Epileptor model.

claim: The Epileptor accounts in principle for only a single dynamotype.
source: However, the Epileptor accounts in principle for only a single dynamotype and is not sufficient to explain the data presented above
evidence: The claim is based on the limitations of the Epileptor model.

claim: The fact that individuals can express different types of seizures over time leads to the prediction that different dynamotypes must coexist in the same model.
source: The fact that individuals can express different types of seizures over time leads to two predictions that must be included within a model of human seizure dynamics: different dynamotypes must coexist in the same model
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the data presented.

claim: The fact that individuals can express different types of seizures over time leads to the prediction that there must be an endogenous mechanism by which the brain can transition slowly between dynamotypes.
source: and there must be an endogenous mechanism by which the brain can transition slowly between dynamotypes.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the data presented.

claim: Previous mathematical work demonstrated that the procedure to build a minimal model for the SN/SH type provides a two-dimensional map for the parameter space of the fast variables on which all the six bifurcations can be placed.
source: Previous mathematical work demonstrated that the procedure to build a minimal model for the SN/SH type (Golubitsky et al., 2001) provides a two-dimensional map for the parameter space of the fast variables on which all the six bifurcations can be placed (Dumortier et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Golubitsky et al., 2001 and Dumortier et al., 1991.

claim: The use of an ultraslow variable allows full exploration of the seizure map.
source: Saggio et al. showed that the use of an ultraslow variable allows full exploration of the map (Saggio et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saggio et al., 2017.

claim: Any brain region able to generate SN/SH seizures can potentially generate other types by navigating to different dynamical regimes.
source: Applying these general mathematical principles to epilepsy implies that any brain region able to generate SN/SH seizures can potentially generate other types by navigating to different dynamical regimes (i.e. changing the parameters of differential equations).
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from mathematical principles.

claim: A large number of physiological neuron and neural population models can be mapped upon a canonical dynamic model under certain mild conditions (existence of a Bogdanov-Takens point).
source: That work also showed that a large number of physiological neuron and neural population models can be mapped upon a canonical dynamic model under certain mild conditions (existence of a Bogdanov-Takens point).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to prior work (Saggio et al., 2017).

claim: All physiological parameters are absorbed in only three generic parameters in the canonical model.
source: All physiological parameters are then absorbed in only three generic parameters, which span a three-dimensional parameter space, in which all bifurcations are represented.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the canonical model.

claim: All neighborhood relations between bifurcations can be displayed as projections onto the spherical surface within the parameter space, yielding a canonical 2D map.
source: Detailed bifurcation analysis reveals that all neighborhood relations between bifurcations can be displayed (without loss of generality) as projections onto the spherical surface within the parameter space, yielding a canonical 2D map (Saggio et al., 2017), shown in Figure 4B–C.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saggio et al., 2017 and illustrated in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The seizure map displays the basic topology of all possible relations between bifurcation lines, including identity of the bifurcation and the organization of its nearest neighborhood including proximity and intersection of bifurcations.
source: This map displays the basic topology of all possible relations between bifurcation lines, including identity of the bifurcation and the organization of its nearest neighborhood including proximity and intersection of bifurcations.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the seizure map.

claim: The navigation of the canonical 2D map through continuous parameter changes selectively generates dynamotypes.
source: The navigation of the canonical 2D map (that is a flat projection of a spherical surface) through continuous parameter changes selectively generates dynamotypes and justifies that we call it a seizure map.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the seizure map.

claim: The state of a brain region at any moment can be represented as a location on the seizure map, which defines its dynamical properties.
source: The state of a brain region at any moment can be represented as a location on the map, which defines its dynamical properties.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the seizure map.

claim: Regions in the seizure map that correspond to different regimes, including quiescent and ictal states, are separated by bifurcation curves.
source: Regions in the map that correspond to different regimes, including quiescent and ictal states, are separated by bifurcation curves.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the seizure map.

claim: Seizures are represented as black arrows on the seizure map, each arrow corresponding to one dynamotype.
source: Seizures are represented as black arrows, each arrow corresponding to one dynamotype.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the seizure map.

claim: Movement along the black arrow on the seizure map is produced by slow mechanisms leading to seizure offset.
source: Movement along the black arrow is produced by slow (of the order of the ictal length) mechanisms leading to seizure offset.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the seizure map.

claim: Ultraslow movements on the seizure map are responsible for changing the location of the brain state while at rest.
source: Ultraslow movements on the seizure map are responsible for changing the location of the brain state while at rest (as may happen during the night and day cycle) and enable the expression of different types of seizures as observed clinically.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the seizure map and provides an explanation for clinical observations.

claim: The seizure map provides a hypothesis to describe how a patient's current state can affect seizure dynamics.
source: and the seizure map provides a hypothesis to describe how a patient's current state (i.e. location on the map) can affect seizure dynamics (whether a seizure is likely to occur, and what type is most likely).
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the seizure map and represents a hypothesis.

claim: Figure 4C depicts paths for seven of the 16 dynamotypes placed on a two-parameter map.
source: Figure 4C depicts paths (black arrows) for seven of the 16 dynamotypes placed on a two-parameter map.
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 4C.

claim: Adding one additional parameter allows the seizure map to be extended and create seven other dynamotypes in three dimensions.
source: Adding one additional parameter allows this map to be extended and create seven other types in three dimensions
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the seizure map and mathematical reasoning.

claim: The final two dynamotypes require even higher dimensions to create.
source: while the final two types require even higher dimensions to create (Saggio et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saggio et al., 2017.

claim: Higher dimensional dynamotypes require very fine parameter tuning, and thus are less likely to occur.
source: These higher dimensional types require very fine parameter tuning, and thus are less likely to occur (Golubitsky et al., 2001; Saggio et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Golubitsky et al., 2001 and Saggio et al., 2017.

claim: TSD in conjunction with the seizure map and choice of slow dynamics can establish a hierarchy of seizures.
source: TSD does not predict the likelihood of dynamotypes, but in conjunction with the seizure map and choice of slow dynamics, a hierarchy of seizures can be established
evidence: The claim is based on the description of TSD and the seizure map.

claim: The hierarchy of seizures predicted by the model is supported by clinical data.
source: which is supported by our clinical data (Appendix II. 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Appendix II.5.

claim: The dynamotypes that occurred the most (e.g. SN/FLC and SN/SH) were predicted to be among the most likely to occur.
source: for instance the dynamotypes that occurred the most (e.g. SN/FLC and SN/SH) were predicted to be among the most likely to occur.
evidence: The claim is supported by the comparison of model predictions with clinical data.

claim: The slow permittivity variable affects the general brain state, or position on the map, on the scale of minutes to hours.
source: The slow permittivity variable affects the general brain state, or position on the map, on the scale of minutes to hours.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the model.

claim: Fast fluctuations on the scale of ms to s are better described as perturbations of the brain state from its current location on the map.
source: There are also fast fluctuations on the scale of ms to s, better described as perturbations of the brain state from its current location on the map.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the model.

claim: Fast perturbations include many physiological phenomena such as afferent signals and neural potentials.
source: These perturbations are modeled as 'noise' within the model, but in reality they also include many physiological phenomena such as afferent signals and neural potentials—in effect anything that perturbs the system (Jirsa et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jirsa et al., 2014.

claim: Both slow and fast fluctuations can lead to seizures by pushing the system across the bifurcation.
source: Both types of fluctuations can lead to seizures by pushing the system across the bifurcation.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the model.

claim: The topology of the seizure map was initially proven mathematically to be generic and rigorously valid for bursting.
source: It is important to note that the topology of the map in Figure 4 was initially proven mathematically to be generic and rigorously valid for bursting (Dumortier et al., 1991; Baer et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dumortier et al., 1991 and Baer et al., 2006.

claim: The invariance of the seizure map topology establishes the ground truth to define the relationships between the different bifurcations in the proximity of the SN/SH type.
source: This invariance establishes the ground truth to define the relationships between the different bifurcations in the proximity of the SN/SH type

claim: Transitions between certain dynamotypes may be more common due to their proximity on the seizure map.
source: which leads to a key prediction: transitions between certain types may be more common due to their proximity on the map.

claim: When bifurcation curves are very close on the seizure map, even small fluctuations in the parameters can cause a transition between types.
source: For example, considering the bistability region in the upper part of the map, we note that the offset curves of SH and SupH approach until they meet. When the curves are very close, even small fluctuations in the parameters can cause a transition between types.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the seizure map.

claim: If fluctuating internal conditions allow individuals to move around regions of convergence on the seizure map, patients may have seizures belonging to different types over time.
source: If fluctuating internal conditions allow individuals to move around these regions of convergence, patients may have seizures belonging to different types over time, as observed in our longitudinal analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the seizure map and provides an explanation for clinical observations.

claim: The model predicts that transitions between specific dynamotypes are more likely to occur if these types are close in the map.
source: The model predicts that transitions between specific types are more likely to occur if these types are close in the map, in the sense just shown of bifurcation curves approaching each other within the same bistability region.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the seizure map.

claim: Transitions between dynamotypes belonging to distant bistability regions require stronger changes in the ultraslow permittivity variable(s) and are thus less likely to occur.
source: On the contrary, transitions between types belonging to distant bistability regions require stronger changes in the ultraslow permittivity variable(s) and are thus less likely to occur.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the seizure map.

claim: Two dynamotypes are paired when they share the same seizure onset or the same offset, and a continuous change of parameters in the seizure map can lead from one type to the other.
source: Two dynamotypes are paired when they share the same seizure onset or the same offset, and a continuous change of parameters in the seizure map can lead from one type to the other, sometimes even during a seizure.

claim: The seizure map predicts possible pairings as motions toward different bifurcations while a seizure is ongoing.
source: The seizure map predicts possible pairings as motions toward different bifurcations while a seizure is ongoing.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the seizure map.

claim: Five examples of seizures switching from SupH to SH/SNIC bifurcation during the seizure were found in the data (out of >2000 seizures).
source: We found five examples of this behavior in our data (out of >2000 seizures) and reproduced it with our model.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model reproduced the behavior of seizures switching from SupH to SH/SNIC bifurcation during the seizure.
source: We found five examples of this behavior in our data (out of >2000 seizures) and reproduced it with our model.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulations.

claim: 100 simulations with an ultraslow drift and noise generated several different dynamotypes, predominantly SN/SH, SupH/SH, and SN/SupH.
source: With these settings, we ran 100 simulations, which generated several different dynamotypes, predominantly SN/SH, SupH/SH, and SN/SupH (Appendix III).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulations presented in Appendix III.

claim: 10 out of 100 simulations had transitions during the seizure from SupH to SH offset, in the same manner as the clinical data.
source: Several had transitions during the seizure from one bifurcation to another, 10 of which in the same manner as the data in Figure 5A, switching from SupH to SH offset.
